title: welcome to Total Vocal Skool community
More Women Than Men Sing Barbershop? Why It Matters
description:
For 88 years, every quartet champion of the Barbershop Harmony Society was male. That streak just ended.

I sat down in a dorm basement at the Harmony Explosion New England camp with two people who have spent their whole lives inside this art form: Steve Tramack, chair of BHS contest and judging, arranger, and lead editor of the "Arranging Barbershop" series — and Renée Tramack, singing judge, two-time international quartet champion, and director of an A-scoring chorus.

GQ just became the first non-male quartet champions in the history of the Barbershop Harmony Society, scoring a perfect 100 from every performance judge with "Mothers and Daughters." Steve has watched them sing it 150 times and still cries.

About 15 years ago, BHS leadership asked me what I saw coming. I told them the single-gender era was going to end one of two ways: by lawsuit, or by their own choice. They chose. They took real blowback for it. This is the payoff.

Two stats most singers have backwards: more women sing barbershop than men, and more people sing it outside the United States than inside. Poland, Israel, Australia, India.

We also go deep on the craft — why forcing barbershop onto SATB fights the harmonic series, why the early repertoire was three chords rooted in gospel, why simpler chords ring more, and how the competition "arrangement arms race" has been making average groups worse.
the

CHAPTERS
00:00 Two lifelong barbershoppers
04:58 GQ and the perfect 100
08:35 The conversation that changed the rules
12:35 More women than men, more outside the US
13:48 Why barbershop breaks SATB
19:10 The arrangement arms race
23:43 What's changing in the barbershop world
24:57 The BHS Judges Studio
26:19 Go hear a rehearsal ring

Barbershop is not a genre of music. It's a style of arranging music. And now the doors are open to everyone.

title: Can You Make a Living in Music? (Yes, Here's How)
description:
Being good will not get you hired. That's the part nobody tells you.

I sat down with Annabelle Ye to talk about the thing music school skips: the business of music. Not theory, not technique — how you actually turn musical skill into a living.

The biggest mistake young arrangers and musicians make is assuming talent is the whole job. "I'm good, so my phone will ring." It won't. You have to spend as much time on the business as you do on the music.

What actually works: publish everything you write on ArrangeMe and price it low so people find your name. Give a group an arrangement plus fifteen minutes of coaching, and one job becomes repeat business, repeat business, repeat business. Start regional, where you can actually be in the room — coaching a rehearsal over Zoom is really hard. And be part of the community, because those personal relationships are where the next opportunity comes from.

My son is 26 and scoring full-length television and film. A lot of his equally talented friends gave up. The difference was never talent. It was working the business.

title: Zagreb Sings Back: A Tunnel, A Market, and a UNESCO Tradition
description:
Every city has a sound. Zagreb's is underground.

Grič Tunnel — a WWII shelter under the old town, now a public passage — has reverb longer than most concert halls. Above ground: klapa, Croatia's own unaccompanied close-harmony tradition, UNESCO-listed since 2012.

A wall in Zagreb reads: your heart rate can sync to the beat of the music you're listening to. That's the whole job. We're not decorating rooms with sound — we're changing what happens inside the people in them.

description:

Submission deadline: January 12th, 2018

Disney Concerts is teaming up with a cappella legend Deke Sharon ("Pitch Perfect" "The Sing Off") and Creative Director Jim Millan ("Kids In The Hall" "Mythbusters Live") to create "D Cappella," a Pentatonix-style vocal performance show built around a 7-voice part group of performers (Soprano, Mezzo, Alto, Tenor, Baritone, Bass, and Vocal Percussion). "D Cappella" will present new, contemporary arrangements of Disney repertoire while interacting with state of the art projections and screens.

Tour will start rehearsing in early March 2018 and performing in late March. All performers will be contracted for the whole initial run, which is approximately 40 performances in performing arts center venues across the country. Base salary is $2000/week. Performers must be legally able to work in the U.S.
